slides.say: A drawer holds ten red, eight blue and six green socks. In the dark, Dana takes out socks one at a time. What is the smallest number of socks she must take out to be sure she has three socks of the same color?

To be sure is the key. Dana can't see the colors, so she has to be ready for the worst luck. [short pause] We'll solve it in two different ways, by understanding the worst luck, and then by plugging in the answers.
at: To be sure is the key

slides.say: [short pause] Let's start by understanding, with a simpler question first. How many socks must she take to be sure of two of the same color, a pair? With bad luck, the first three socks are red, blue and green, one of each. She still has no pair.
But the fourth sock has to be red, blue or green. Whatever it is, it matches a sock she already has. So three socks can fail, and four always work.

That's the rule for to be sure questions. Imagine the worst luck, the longest she can go without what she wants. Then add one more. Why plus one? The worst luck is the most socks she can take and still fail. One more sock, and failing is impossible.

Here's another example. To be sure of four socks of one color, the worst luck is three of each color. Three plus three plus three is nine socks. And still there are no four of one color. So she needs nine plus one, ten.
at: To be sure of four socks
So she needs nine plus one

slides.say: Now our question, three of the same color. Careful, it's any color, not three red socks. For three red socks, all eight blue and all six green could come out first. Eight plus six plus three is seventeen. How long can she avoid it? With the worst luck she gets two of every color. Two plus two plus two is six socks. And still no color has three.
The seventh sock is red, blue or green, and that color reaches three. So six socks can fail, and seven always work. Choice number two is our answer.
at: Choice number two is our answer

slides.say: [pause] Now let's plug in the answers. They ask for the smallest number that makes her sure. So we start from the smallest choice and go up. The first one that always works is the answer.
Choice number four, four socks. Can four socks fail to give three of a color? They can. Two red, one blue and one green have no three of a color. So four isn't enough, and choice number four is out.
at: and choice number four is out

slides.say: Now choice number two, seven socks. Can seven socks avoid three of a color? To avoid it, each color can give at most two. Three colors with two each is only six socks. Seven is more than six, so one color must reach three. Seven always works.
Nine and seventeen are bigger than seven, and we want the smallest number that is sure. Choice number two is our answer, and I'll see you in the next question.
